docs.title: Mandate — attested, revisioned spending authority for autonomous agents
docs.html:
Working title. The name is contested: at least four other agent-authority projects use "Mandate" (docs.mandate.md, mandate.help, runmandate.xyz, mandate-agent.com). Decision D-015 records the collision and docs/PENDING-HUMAN.md H-10 asks the sponsor to pick a new name before the repo goes public. Nothing in this document depends on the name.

Status: testnet prototype, not deployed. One Rust contract, one static console, one deterministic replay. No mainnet funds, no audit, no custody. Section 9 lists exactly what is implemented and what is not.

1. Abstract

An autonomous agent needs the ability to spend. Giving it a funded wallet gives it the ability to spend everything, on anything, for any reason. The usual answers — session keys, spending caps, an allowlist checked inside the agent's own process, a policy engine behind an API — all move the decision somewhere the owner has to trust, and several of them move it into the same process the attacker already controls.

This paper describes a different placement. The owner creates a mandate: a policy object plus a funded balance held by a contract. The agent holds a NEAR FunctionCall access key scoped to one method on that contract. Every spend is a contract call. The contract checks the allowlist, the per-transaction, per-day and per-counterparty ceilings, and the balance it already holds. Above a threshold, the spend becomes a stored request a human answers later. Every spend above zero must carry an attestation: the hash of the decision that produced it, the measurement of the code that made the decision, and the policy revision it was decided under. The contract refuses a spend whose intent does not hash to the attested intent, whose decision hash was already used, whose code measurement is not the one the policy allows, or whose policy revision is not the one currently in force.

The claim is narrow and testable: a spend is rejected unless its decision hash matches the attested hash (C5), and a decision is bound to the policy revision it was made under (C15). Both are demonstrated by a deterministic replay of fifteen events against the real contract, and both can be recomputed in a browser without trusting our server.

2. The problem

2.1 Authority is not the same as a limit

A limit answers "how much". Authority answers "how much, to whom, on which chain, under which rules, decided by which code, and can I see afterwards that it was respected". Session keys and token allowances answer the first question. They do not answer the rest, and they do not survive a policy amendment: a signed allowance is valid until it is revoked, whatever the owner's intentions have become since.

2.2 Comparison-gating is the wrong primitive

The intuitive design is to let a signing quorum compare the requested amount against a budget before signing. IACR ePrint 2026/2176 shows that comparison gating admits a deterministic bypass. This project therefore treats a budget as a funded balance, not a comparison: the contract holds the money, so the amount it can authorise is bounded by what it has, not by a number it agreed to respect (D-002, C7).

2.3 The decision usually lives where the attacker lives

In an agent wallet that enforces policy in the agent's process, or in a library the agent imports, prompt injection is not a policy bypass — it is a policy rewrite. The attacker does not need to defeat the check; it only needs the check to run with the attacker's inputs. Moving enforcement one layer out, into a contract the agent cannot modify, changes the shape of the attack: the agent can still be manipulated into asking for something, but the answer is decided by code the owner deployed.

3. Where this sits relative to what exists

The idea is not new, and pretending otherwise would fail the first search a security-literate judge runs. The distinction is where the check runs and what a third party can verify afterwards.

SystemEnforcesBudget modelWhat the owner must trustAttested reason per spend
NEAR Intents Agent API (official, 2026)rules + grant signed by the owner, executed by an attested TEE serviceUSD accounting inside the servicethe operator and its TEE attestationyes, per execution
TEE agent wallets (enclave-signed)policy inside the enclavewallet balancethe enclave vendoryes
near-agent-guard (offline prototype, same track)a CLI guard over proposed actionspolicy counters in the processthe process; no key is createdno chain enforcement
ERC-7715 session keys (Ethereum)scoped key permissionsallowancethe account implementationno
Mandate (this repo)a NEAR contract, called by a scoped keyfunded balance held by the contractthe contract code you can readhash equality enforced on-chain

Two honest conclusions follow. First, the Intents Agent API is more capable than this prototype: it settles across 35+ chains, it has an owner-facing product, and it runs in production infrastructure. Mandate is not a replacement for it and does not claim to be. Second, the difference that survives is verifiability: here the enforcement is a contract method a judge can call, every refusal is a typed code a judge can grep, and the console recomputes the hashes in the browser. If the question is "which one would an operator deploy tomorrow", the answer is the Intents API. If the question is "which one can I check without trusting an operator", this is the smaller, inspectable instance of the same idea.

4. Design

4.1 Objects

  • Mandate — owner, agent account, policy, policy hash, revision counter,

policy history, funded balance, spent totals, per-counterparty totals, day index, suspension flag, settlement map.

  • Policy — version, asset, expiry block, allowlist of (chain, counterparty,

label), per-transaction / per-day / per-counterparty-per-day ceilings, an escalation threshold, and whether an attestation is required (plus the code measurement allowed to decide).

  • Attestation — decision hash, code hash, quote hash, policy hash, intent

hash.

  • Authorization — what spend returns: mandate id, intent hash, amount,

asset, chain, counterparty, decision hash, policy hash, status.

  • PendingRequest — an escalation: the same intent, held for a human.
  • PolicyRevision — revision number, hash, block, and the four limits that

were in force.

4.2 The funded balance

create_mandate is payable: the attached deposit becomes the balance. fund can add to it. Nothing in the contract can create balance, and spend refuses an amount above the balance. The owner's exposure is bounded by what they deposited, which is a property of the ledger rather than of an arithmetic check.

4.3 The decision, hashed and bound

The intent hash is the SHA-256 of a canonical JSON tuple {amount, asset, chain, vendor} with sorted keys. The attestation presents the intent the enclave decided on. spend recomputes the tuple from its own arguments and refuses a mismatch, so an agent cannot obtain a decision for a cheap action and then widen the amount.

The decision hash is recorded in a used-set. A decision authorises one spend, once. Escalation and approval deliberately share one decision (D-005): approval answers the stored request, it is not a second decision.

4.4 Policy revisions

update_policy validates the new policy, increments policy_rev, appends a PolicyRevision, and leaves balance and counters untouched — tightening a policy cannot forgive past spend, and loosening one cannot create funds.

Because every attestation names the policy hash it was decided under, an amendment invalidates decisions taken before it. The same rule applies to a pending escalation: a request raised under revision n cannot be approved once the mandate is at revision n+1; it must be asked again. This is the property the demo's events 13–15 exist to show, and the reason policy_changed is a refusal code rather than a warning.

4.5 Escalation

Above escalate_over, spend stores a PendingRequest and returns pending. No debit happens at request time. The owner calls approve (debit now) or reject (never). This is a stored request, not a paused call: the window for a human is unbounded, and a timeout cannot corrupt state.

4.6 Settlement

An authorisation is not a transfer. A separate attestor account calls settle with the intent hash and a foreign transaction reference; the contract records it once. An authorisation with no settlement is visibly unfinished, which is what the fourth stage of the proof rail represents.

5. Check order

The order is part of the specification, because it decides which code a judge sees first.

  1. suspension
  2. expiry block
  3. asset equality
  4. chain enabled
  5. counterparty allowed
  6. amount non-zero
  7. per-transaction ceiling
  8. day rollover, then per-day ceiling
  9. per-counterparty ceiling
  10. funded balance
  11. attestation: present, code hash, policy revision, decision unused,

intent match

  1. escalation threshold, or debit and authorise

Every failure panics with PolicyViolation: <code>; detail is logged separately as violation: <code>: <detail>, so the machine-readable word is never buried in prose. The vocabulary is frozen at 21 codes and each is asserted by a test.

6. Threat model

AdversaryCapabilityResultResidual risk
Injected agentcan call spend with arbitrary argumentscannot exceed the policy or the balance; cannot name a counterparty that is not allowlisted; cannot widen an attested intentthe agent can still spend within its authority on a bad reason; that is a policy question, not this contract's
Injected agent, key theftholds the scoped keythe key cannot transfer, add keys, delete the account, or call another contracta stolen key spends the remaining balance within the policy until the owner suspends
Agent replaying a decisionre-presents an old attestationdecision_replayednone within one deployment
Agent riding an amendmentpresents a decision made under an older policypolicy_changednone; the decision must be re-made
Compromised attestorcan write arbitrary settlement referencescannot move funds; can mislabel which foreign tx settled an intentsettlement references are attestor-asserted, not proven on-chain
Lying operatoredits the console or the snapshotthe browser recomputes the policy and intent hashes; a mismatch is showna judge who reads only the screenshot is trusting the screenshot
Malicious ownerchanges the policy mid-flightrevisions are recorded; old decisions stop workingthe owner is trusted by definition

Explicit non-goals: this contract does not verify a hardware quote, does not bridge assets, does not hold a private key for another chain, and cannot prevent an owner from suspending a mandate at an inconvenient moment.

7. Determinism and replay

make demo executes a fixed fifteen-event scenario against the real contract in near-sdk's test VM. Block height and timestamp are constants, amounts are integers, and no wall clock is read, so the emitted JSON is byte-identical on any machine. The snapshot hash is printed by make demo; the console reads that same file and nothing else.

The replay is not a simulation of the contract; it is the contract, with a recording of the views after each call. That distinction is what lets the console show a refusal code that a test also asserts, and it is why the console contains no arithmetic about money.

8. Evaluation

Measured, on 2026-11-06:

CheckResult
contract unit tests (cargo test in rust:1)27 passed, 0 failed
replay events15, final balance 56.000000 USDC, 0 pending
tools/verify.mjs13 checks, inputsHash stable across runs
browser verification12 rows recomputed with WebCrypto, all agree
Playwright + axe14 tests, zero WCAG A/AA violations on all six routes, no horizontal overflow at 380px on any route
wasm build155 KB release artifact

No latency or cost claims are made here: the contract has never been deployed, so any number would be invented.

9. What is implemented, and what is not

Implemented: the contract and its views, the deterministic replay, the console (six routes, replay player, in-browser hash recomputation, CSV, print receipt, policy revision table), the refusal vocabulary, the docs pipeline, the e2e suite.

Not implemented, and labelled as such wherever it would otherwise appear: a testnet deployment and a real transaction link (blocked on a funded FunctionCall key, H-6), a hardware-quote verifier, the attestor worker, the cross-chain signer, the Bond submission (deferred, D-011), self-hosted fonts (D-012).

10. Related work

  • NEAR Intents Agent API — owner-signed rules and grant, TEE-attested execution.
  • NEAR FunctionCall access keys — the key-scoping primitive this design relies on.
  • ERC-7715 / ERC-7710 — scoped permissions and delegation on Ethereum.
  • IACR ePrint 2026/2176 — the comparison-gating bypass that motivates balances.
  • near-agent-guard — a same-track offline guard; useful as a policy-expression

reference, not as enforcement.

11. Limitations

  1. One asset per mandate in v1.
  2. Per-counterparty totals are cleared on day rollover, which is correct for the

limits but loses history; the console shows the current day only.

  1. The used-decision set grows without bound; a production deployment needs

pruning or a per-revision scope.

  1. The policy hash covers the policy object, not the contract code. A code

upgrade is a different trust question, addressed by the code hash for the deciding service.

  1. Settlement is asserted by one attestor account. A quorum of attestors is the

obvious next step and is not implemented.

12. Reproducing the claims

make dev      # console, no secrets, no network at runtime
make demo     # fifteen events, expected table printed before comparison
make verify   # recompute policy, intent and revision invariants
make test     # 27 contract tests (or make test-linux with Docker)
make e2e      # 14 Playwright + axe tests
make doctor   # ACTIVE / FALLBACK per module, honestly

Every claim in this paper maps to a row in docs/CLAIMS.md and to a command or a test. If a claim loses its proof, the claim is deleted rather than softened.

docs.title: ARCHITECTURE — Mandate (as built)
docs.html:
What exists in this repository, in the order an engineer would read it. Diagrams live in docs/UML.md; the claims live in docs/CLAIMS.md. Anything described here can be pointed at a file.

1. Shape

One Rust contract, one static console, one deterministic replay, four Node tools. No server-side rendering, no database, no key material in the repository, no network call at runtime.

mandate/
  contracts/mandate/src/
    lib.rs        the contract: owner paths, agent path, views
    state.rs      stored types and the JSON return types
    policy.rs     the policy object, its hash, its validation
    errors.rs     PolicyViolation + the frozen code list
    util.rs       sha256, intent_hash, storage helpers
    tests.rs      27 unit tests, one per failure path plus the happy paths
    demo.rs       the fifteen-event scenario (writes the snapshot)
  console/
    index.html    shell: context bar, tabs, canvas, proof rail
    styles.css    the whole visual system (tokens at the top)
    app.js        reads snapshot.json + docs.json; renders; recomputes hashes
    data/
      snapshot.json   committed replay (generated by make demo)
      docs.json       generated from markdown by make docs
  docs/
    SCREENER.md   the hostile-reviewer path
    ARCHITECTURE.md  this file

Everything under tools/ is dependency-free Node: serve-console.mjs, demo-report.mjs, verify.mjs, doctor.mjs, build-docs.mjs.

2. Contract surface

PathCallerEffect
new(attestor)deployerowner = predecessor, stores the attestor account
create_mandate(agent, policy) payableownerbalance = deposit; policy hash; revision 1
fund(id) payableowneradds to the balance
suspend(id) / resume(id)ownerthe kill switch, a flag
update_policy(id, policy)ownernew hash, revision + 1, history append
spend(id, chain, amount, asset, vendor, attestation)agentthe whole check order, then debit or escalate
approve(request_id) / reject(request_id)owneranswers a stored escalation
settle(id, intent, tx_ref)attestorrecords the foreign tx once
get_mandate, list_mandatesanyonemandate views
list_pending, get_pendinganyonethe escalation queue
get_settlement, get_policy_historyanyonesettlement and revisions
stats, heldanyonecounters and the total the contract holds

The UI never computes money: every figure it prints is a field from one of those views. held() exists so the console can show custody without summing in JS.

Every refusal logs violation: <code> before it panics (D-018). The release profile uses panic = "abort", so an on-chain failure arrives as a wasm unreachable trap with no message; the log line is what lets a stranger read the typed code in the block explorer instead of taking our word for it.

3. Data and invariants

State: owner, attestor, mandates: BTreeMap<id, Mandate>, pending: BTreeMap<request_id, PendingRequest>, used_decisions: BTreeMap<decision_hash, bool>, next_id: u64.

Invariants, each with a test:

  1. balance + spent_total == deposit_total for every mandate.
  2. policy_rev == policy_history.len().
  3. policy_history.last().hash == policy_hash.
  4. A decision hash appears at most once in used_decisions.
  5. spent_day + value <= per_day and `spent_by_counterparty[k] + value <=

per_counterparty_day` after every authorised spend.

  1. A settlement exists at most once per (mandate, intent).

The day window is block_timestamp / 86_400_000. On rollover, spent_day resets and the per-counterparty map is cleared. That is correct for the limits and is listed as a limitation in the whitepaper: history is not retained per day.

4. Check order

suspended → expired → asset → chain → vendor → amount>0 → per_tx →
day rollover → per_day → per_counterparty → balance → attestation
(present → code hash → policy revision → decision unused → intent match) →
escalate or debit

The order is deliberate: the cheapest and most legible refusals come first, and the attestation checks come last so a bad amount is reported as an amount problem, not as an attestation problem. docs/UML.md §7 draws this.

Two families of code are easy to confuse:

  • attestation_mismatch — same revision, but the intent the enclave decided on is

not the intent being asked for (amount, vendor, chain, asset).

  • policy_changed — the decision is internally consistent, but it was made under

a policy revision that is no longer current.

5. Hashing

policy.hash() is SHA-256 over serde_json::to_string(&policy). Field order is fixed by the struct, U128 serialises as a decimal string, so the byte sequence is reproducible in Rust, Node and the browser. tools/verify.mjs and app.js#renderVerify both recompute it from policyJson in the snapshot.

intent_hash(chain, amount, vendor, asset) is SHA-256 over {"amount":"…","asset":"…","chain":"…","vendor":"…"} — sorted keys, so JSON key order cannot change the digest.

The attestor, not the contract, is responsible for the quote hash. The contract compares a hash; it does not verify Intel's signature. Every document repeats that sentence because the difference matters.

6. Determinism

demo.rs fixes block height (4 120 001…4 120 016) and timestamp (1 700 000 000 000 000 000), uses integer amounts, and never reads the wall clock or a random source. The snapshot therefore hashes identically on every machine; make demo prints the hash, and a change means something non-deterministic entered the scenario.

The release test also asserts the refusal codes it expects: a scenario that silently starts succeeding fails the demo instead of recording a misleading step.

7. Console

app.js fetches two documents: data/snapshot.json (contract views per event) and data/docs.json (markdown rendered at build time by tools/build-docs.mjs). It renders six routes from them; it has no other data source.

  • #/desk — the replay: strip, event card, timeline, mandate table, queue.
  • #/mandate — limits, allowlist, policy revisions, attestation, settlement.
  • #/verify — recomputes policy and intent hashes and the revision invariants.
  • #/refusals — the frozen vocabulary, marking which codes the run produced.
  • #/paper — whitepaper, architecture and diagrams, from the same markdown the

repository ships.

  • #/about — scope, non-claims, keyboard map.

The proof rail is a four-cell record of one event's lifecycle: policy → attest → authorise → settle. A cell stays empty when its stage did not happen; that is the point of having four cells instead of a single "success" badge.

Accessibility is a gate, not a courtesy: axe runs on every route with the WCAG 2.0/2.1/2.2 A and AA tags, focus rings are measured, the rail collapses below 960px, nothing scrolls sideways at 380px, and reduced motion turns the replay into a jump to the end.

8. Tools

ToolContract it keeps
serve-console.mjsserves console/ with Cache-Control: no-store; /health for readiness
demo-report.mjsprints the expected table before comparing; fails on one mismatch
verify.mjsrecomputes 13 checks from the snapshot, prints a stable inputsHash
doctor.mjsACTIVE / FALLBACK per module, exits 1 on any fallback
build-docs.mjsmarkdown → docs.json; escapes everything, no HTML passthrough
render-diagrams.mjsMermaid → committed SVG; the only tool that uses a package, and not on the make dev path
verify-lib.mjsthe 13 checks, once, shared by verify.mjs, the API and the MCP server
api.mjsthe read model: formats snapshot fields, adds no money
api-server.mjsscoped bearer keys, typed JSON errors, read-only
keystore.mjs / keys.mjsSHA-256 key store and its CLI; the secret is printed once
mcp-server.mjsthe six read-only tools over JSON-RPC on stdio

None of the first five need npm install. Playwright is used only by make e2e, and render-diagrams.mjs needs Mermaid as well; both are development steps, and their outputs (screenshots, SVG) are committed so a fresh clone renders the same page.

8.1 The control plane (HTTP and MCP)

The console is one client of the snapshot, not the owner of it. Two more clients are in this repository, both read-only, both behind a scope check:

  • tools/api-server.mjs — GET /v1/{status,mandates,pending,stats,policy}

(read:views), /v1/events[/:index] (read:events), /v1/verify (read:verify). A bearer key is required; 401 distinguishes unauthorized from key_revoked, 403 is scope_missing, 405 refuses every non-GET, and /health is the only unauthenticated route.

  • tools/mcp-server.mjs — the same views as six MCP tools over stdio. No

network, no dependency, no key: it runs where the repository is.

Keys live in mandate/console/data/api-keys.json (gitignored): id, label, scopes, prefix, SHA-256 of the secret, revoked flag. A fresh clone has no file and therefore no clients, which is why make test-api mints its own keys in a temporary store. Rate limiting is per key, in memory, and the API holds no signer: there is no code path from either surface to a transaction.

9. Deployment (done on testnet, 2026-11-06)

Contract: mandate-hackaton-7c1a.testnet (explorer).

StepTransaction

new(attestor)6DYjXWBSW5VkW5Mm3sXaqxavcdvvu6GqgqZ5o6Ly279q
create_mandate (m1)BMxsh2Kfer3USrF5vcTr1iiGWXKu29opGELgdiLyUTr6
create_mandate (m4, current)7Km9VYd7ttZmk4vijgBxo9p1mzs5qLVAU8bSYPAnxjsv

make chain-demo then drives a second mandate whose agent is the same account: a matching spend is authorised, a spend whose attestation names a different amount is refused on chain, and the authorised intent is settled. The record it writes (console/data/chain.json) is what the Verify page renders; the snapshot the other routes render stays a replay, and both say which they are.

The original plan, for reference

  1. Fund a testnet account, add a FunctionCall key scoped to

mandate.testnet::spend.

  1. cargo near deploy (or near deploy with the release wasm).
  2. create_mandate with a small deposit; record the transaction id.
  3. Set MANDATE_CONTRACT; make doctor flips the deployment row to ACTIVE.
  4. Put the explorer links in SCREENER.md §0. The console build line stays a

replay statement (replay of a contract run, not a chain read) because the console still renders the snapshot; the deployed account and its transactions are rendered from console/data/chain.json on the Verify page, so the two claims never borrow each other's authority.

Until step 4 happens, every surface says replay and the build line says never deployed, and make doctor exits 1. That is intentional: a green doctor or a live-looking build line with no deployment would be a lie.

10. Extension points

  • Multiple assets per mandate — policy carries one asset in v1; the balance

and counters are already per-mandate, so this is a policy shape change.

  • Attestor quorum — settle is a single-account call; a threshold set is the

natural next step and changes one function.

  • Revocation by key deletion — the account-level kill switch is outside the

contract; the contract's suspend is the in-band equivalent and needs no key operation.

  • Bond — the deferred second submission (D-011) shares the policy and

attestation types, not the code: copy, never import (D-004).

docs.title: UML and flow diagrams
docs.html:
Mermaid blocks render on GitHub and in most editors. The console's Paper route shows the same diagrams as source, because a static, offline page cannot run a renderer without adding a dependency (D-012, D-016). The prose beside each diagram is the authoritative part; the picture is a convenience.

Contents: component view · spend sequence · refusal sequence · policy amendment sequence · mandate state machine · data model · check order · deployment.

1. Component view

The console never writes and holds no key. The only writer paths are the three accounts above; the only cross-chain fact in the system is the settlement reference, which is asserted rather than proven.

2. Sequence: an authorised spend

3. Sequence: prompt injection is refused

4. Sequence: an amendment invalidates older decisions

This is demo events 13–15. It is also the reason approve re-checks the policy hash: a request queued under revision 1 is refused after the amendment.

5. State machine

Expired and Closed are conditions evaluated at call time, not stored states: the contract refuses with mandate_expired or budget_exhausted and leaves the record readable. A suspended mandate never loses its balance or its counters.

6. Data model

The used-decision set is a flat map decision_hash -> true; it enforces "one decision, one spend" across all mandates in the deployment.

7. Check order

8. Deployment

The local path is what a screener gets. The testnet path is written down with its blocker rather than mocked.
